title: TICKETMASTER
subtitle: Millions of people arrive for one on-sale, and no seat may ever be sold twice.
footer: DDIA: Ch 7 write skew · Ch 8 leases / TTL

items: Browsing is huge, read-only traffic that can be slightly stale: cache it hard.
Hold a seat with one atomic conditional update so two buyers can never both win.
For huge on-sales, a virtual waiting room admits users at the rate the system can handle.
View events and seat maps
Search events
Book tickets: pick seats, hold, pay, confirm
Never double-book a seat (strong consistency)
Browse and search highly available, low latency
Extreme spikes: ~10M users for one on-sale
Seat hold ~10 minutes during checkout
Hot event: 10M users, 100k seats.
Reads are massive; successful bookings are capped by seat count (100k).
Protect the booking path from the read storm.

Naive: check the seat is free, then insert a booking. Two users read "free" at the same time and both book: write skew.

items: Hold atomically: UPDATE tickets SET status=HELD, user=?, hold_expires=now()+10m WHERE id=? AND (status=AVAILABLE OR hold_expires < now()).
The user pays with Stripe; the idempotent webhook flips HELD → BOOKED. An expired hold frees itself, with no cron job.
For hot on-sales, a virtual waiting room admits users in batches; the CDN serves pages and Elasticsearch handles search, keeping the booking DB small and safe.
Two users click the same seat?
A conditional update on the ticket row (the seat row materializes the conflict, DDIA Ch 7). Exactly one gets 1 row updated.
Release abandoned holds?
The expiry is part of the condition, or a Redis TTL. No background job is needed for correctness.
Taylor Swift spike?
Waiting room queue (Redis sorted set by arrival), push "your turn" via SSE, admit at the rate booking can handle.
Stale seat map?
Cache for a few seconds; the booking path is the source of truth.
Holding a DB transaction or row lock open while the user pays for 10 minutes.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
